newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cabinet changes not seen before Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Czech cabinet changes not seen before Thursday.

text.p: Senior Czech ministers pondered on Wednesday which of their colleagues might face the axe after leaders of the ruling coalition agreed to recast the beleaguered cabinet.

Leaders of the three parties in the ruling centre-right coalition scheduled a meeting for Thursday to discuss a shakeup of the cabinet after agreeing that a change was needed amid slumping approval ratings and an economic downturn.
With politicians and media guessing which of the 16 ministers might be sacked, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus pleaded with members of parliament not to over-dramatise the situation.
"Partial imbalances and ups-and-downs of the economy are typical for any market economy," Klaus told parliament.

"They will repeat in the future regardless of the political colour of the government. Therefore the government refuses to speak about economic crisis because our current economic situation is very far from crisis."

Last month, Klaus announced a package of measures aimed at giving fresh impetus to economic growth, curbing trade and current account deficits and clamping down on economic crime. It included cuts in public spending and limits on wage growth.
A late night meeting which ended in the early hours of Wednesday failed to strike a deal on which ministerial positions would be affected.
The hastily-arranged meeting headed by Klaus, leader the senior Civic Democratic Party (ODS), came as criticism of post-Communist Europe's most durable governing coalition gathered pace.

Approval ratings for the government and especially Klaus's ODS have dropped recently because of a slowdown in economic performance, some highly publicised cases of financial crime and problems in the health care and education sectors.

Polls put most of the blame for the situation on Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik and Minister of Industry and Trade Vladimir Dlouhy who last week suggested that the whole cabinet should accept the blame for the situation and resign.
"I'm not saying... that negative development in some areas is not important and that the government would close its eyes face to face with it," Klaus told parliament.

Macroeconomic problems -- mainly a current account deficit of more than nine percent of gross domestic product and falling industrial output -- have cut the value of the Czech crown on foreign exchange markets.
The currency has also been hit by worries about political instability. The central bank intervened several times last week to support it.

Czech Radio quoted political sources as saying one proposal under discussion was for Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec to replace Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik, with former ambassador to the United States Michael Zantovsky taking over as foreign minister.
This report could not be independently confirmed.
